section: 3.1 de Duve: a Biochemical View of Life
text:
3.1 de Duve: a Biochemical View of Life
In his Book “Life Evolving - Molecules, Mind and Meaning”, De Duve (2002) gave a very simple but brilliant definition of life:
Life is

One,
Chemistry, and
Information

In the following sections we will explore what de Duve meant with each component in his definition.

title: Position of the course
text:
3.2 Life is One
Life is one because all living organisms on earth

are built of cells
evolved from the same species, LUCA, our last universal common ancestor
use the same molecule for storing, converting and using energy
use the same biological building blocks: lipids, sugars, amino acids for proteins and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).


3.2.1 All Living Organisms are Built of Cells
“Life is One” because all organisms are composed of cells. Green algae that can perform photosynthesis are a beautiful example of unicellular organisms. They were key for the development of life on our planet by releasing oxygen in our atmosphere (Figure 1).








Figure 1: Cyanobacteria, unicellullar organisms that can perform photosynthesis. They were key in the development of life and radically changed Earth by releasing oxygen to our atmosphere (Source: Chisholm Lab, Wikipedia)





A vital component of a cell is its membrane (the outer layer of the cell) that is separating them from their environment while enabling them to interact with it and to concentrate chemicals inside the cell.
Multicellular organisms are composed of multiple cells. The cells are organised in tissues, e.g. spongy tissue in our bones or epithelium cells of our stomach; organs, e.g. bones or our stomach; organ systems, e.g. skeleton or digestive system; up to the organism. Figure 2 also shows how organisms are further organised in populations of organisms, ecosystems, and eventually our entire Biosphere. So “Life is One” because all living organisms consist of cells that are organised in large networks that work together.








Figure 2: Multicellular organisms and biological organisation (Source: mrssmithsbiology)







Last Universal Common Ancestor
“Life is One” because all species evolved from the same ancestral population of cells. This is also referred to as the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA). It is nicely indicated by the tree of life in Figure 3, which is one of the most important organising principles in biology. It shows the evolutionary relationships among different organisms and that all living beings eventually can be traced back to LUCA who is located at the root of the tree. Note, that the animal kingdom to which we belong is only a small branch in the tree.








Figure 3: The tree of life is one of the most important organising principles in biology. It shows the evolutionary relationships among different organisms and also that all living beings eventually can be traced back to the last universal common ancestor (LUCA), who is located at the root of the tree (Source: Wikipedia)







Energy coin
“Life is One” because all living organisms use the same “energy coin”, the ATP-ADP system, to store and reuse energy. Adenosine-triphosphate (ATP) consists of a ribose sugar with 3 phosphate groups and a base adenine. Splitting a phosphate group from adenosine-triphosphate (ATP) results in adenosine-diphosphate (ADP), a free phosphate group and energy. The other way around, energy can be stored as chemical energy by binding a phosphate group to ADP (see Figure 4).
Note, that ATP is also used to build RNA, an important molecule involved in storing, passing and expressing our genetic information. Indeed, ATP is incorporated in RNA upon splitting two phosphate groups. The resulting AMP (adenosine monophosphate) is one of the building blocks of RNA. See Section 3.2.1.7 for more details on RNA. So there is a close link between energy and genetic information!








Figure 4: Our energy coin ATP-ADP. Adenosine-triphosphate (ATP) consists of a base adenine, a ribose sugar and 3 phosphate groups. Splitting a phosphate group from adenosine-triphosphate (ATP) by a reaction with water (H\(_2\)O) results in adenosine-diphosphate (ADP), a free phosphate group and releases energy. The other way around, energy can be stored as chemical energy by binding a phosphate group to ADP (Source: Adapted from Wikipedia)








Building Blocks of Life
“Life is One” because all living organisms are composed of the same basic bio-molecules and we all know more than we think about them because we are what we eat!
Almost all molecules of living organisms are composed of

Lipids, oil and fats, for storage and as building blocks for membranes,
Carbohydrates, sugars, for storing energy and as a backbone of large bio-molecules,
Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, which are the workhorses of a cell and facilitate the majority of its chemical reactions, and
Nucleic Acids, building blocks of RNA and DNA, which are used to store and use the genetic information we inherit from our parents.



Lipids
Lipids, fats and oils, are used for

storage of energy,
regulation of hormones,
transmission of nerve impulses,
cushion vital organs and
transport of fat-soluble nutrients.

Moreover, an important class of lipids, the phospholipids, make up membranes of cells and subcellular compartments called organelles see Figure 5. Indeed phospholipids have a polar head that likes to be in water and a long apolar tail that does not mix with water. Therefore bilayers of phospholipid molecules are spontaneously formed in aqueous solutions.








Figure 5: Phospho-lipids have a very important role in life as they form membranes. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head that likes to mix with water and long hydrophobic tails that do not mix with water. They spontaneously give rise to bilayers in aqueous solutions similar to the structure seen in membranes. Membranes are the boundaries of the cell and they allow passive diffusion of small molecules through their bilayer. Larger molecules can be actively exchanged with the environment through membrane proteins (Source: Doug Hatfield, Wikipedia)






Membranes provide the basis for concentrating specific molecules in (compartments of) living cells. This enable cells to build up a disequilibrium of chemical molecules that can perform work as a concentration gradient spontaneously dissipates toward its equilibrium value. So phospholipids are key for creating the boundary conditions necessary for cellular organization.


Carbohydrates
Carbohydrates are important bio-molecules that are used for

storage,
energy and
structure (Figure 6).









Figure 6: Carbohydrates perform the important functions of storage, energy source and structure. They can be organised in biopolymers, long chains of carbohydrate molecules that are bound together. The polysaccharides starch and glycogen for instance are used to store energy by plant and animal cells, respectively. Cellulose, on the other hand, is a polysaccharide that gives plants structure. Deoxyribose and ribose are important carbohydrates that form the backbone of the biopolymers DNA and RNA, respectively. (Source: thebiologynotes.com)






Storage: glucose is stored inside animal cells using glycogen, a polymer of thousands of glucose molecules that are bound to each-other. Plants use a similar molecule, starch.
Energy source: specific proteins can split glycogen and starch into glucose that is subsequently metabolized for energy.
Structure: carbohydrates form the backbone of many bio-molecules, e.g. long chains of desoxyribose and ribose act as the backbone of the bio-polymers DNA and RNA, respectively; and glucose is the backbone of cellulose, which give plants structure.





Amino Acids
Amino Acids are the building blocks of proteins. Proteins are the main workhorses of the cell and they are important for

moving food,
digesting food,
copying DNA,
for giving the cell structure,
affecting the rates at which other proteins work,
etc…

Amino acids by themselves are simple molecules (Figure 7). Although hundreds of amino acids exist in nature, life is using only 20 of them and it is combining them in long molecules, polymers, which are referred to as proteins. Proteins are hetero-polymers, consisting of the 20 amino acids that are arranged in long sequences that differ from protein to protein. So unlike starch, that only consists of glucose molecules that are all identical, proteins are capable of carrying information.








Figure 7: Amino acids are simple molecules. They can be combined in long molecules, polymers, also known as proteins. Their long chain of amino acids spontaneously folds into a complex 3D structure from which their biological function emerges (Source: thebiologynotes.com)





The crux of proteins is that their long chain of amino acids spontaneously folds into a complex 3D structure, which is determined by the properties and the specific sequence of its amino acids. From their complex and specific 3D structure their biological function emerges.
Indeed, many proteins work as a “lock” in which specific (bio)molecules fit as a “key”. This enables proteins to bring molecules close together and to promote chemical reactions without being consumed. This process is also referred to as catalysis and proteins that perform catalysis are called enzymes, see Figure 8.








Figure 8: Diagram of a protein performing an enzyme action (Source: Wikipedia)







Nucleic Acids
Nucleic acids are built of nucleotides. Each nucleotide is composed of one of four nitrogen-containing nucleobases, which carry the information

cytosine [C],
guanine [G],
adenine [A] or
thymine [T] (DNA) or uracil [U] (RNA) ,

a phosphate group and a sugar, i.e. ribose in ribonucleic acid (RNA, Figure 10) and deoxyribose in deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA, Figure 11).
These nucleotides are the building blocks that are combined in long polymers: RNA and DNA. DNA and RNA are hetero-polymers and the nucleotides conceptually can be combined in any order. So they can contain information. Indeed, they are key to store and use the genetic information we inherit from our parents.
DNA typically occurs as a double strand, where C and G, and, A and T hybridize to each other using respectively three and two hydrogen bridges to form the iconic double stranded helix structure, see Figure 11.
There is a general consensus that life probably began by using RNA as information carrier. DNA, however, is much more stable and lasts longer in water than RNA. Therefore, DNA probably emerged later and is now used to store the genetic information in most organisms.
Life is also one because we share the same genetic code, but we refer to Section 3.4 “Life is Information” for more details.








Figure 9: Nucleic acid: RNA (left) and DNA (right). RNA appears typically in a single strand and DNA as a double stranded molecule (Source: Wikipedia)













Figure 10: RNA is a polymeric molecule with various biological roles in coding, decoding, regulation and expression of genes. RNA consists of a chain of nucleotides. Each nucleotide is build from a ribose sugar that forms the backbone of the RNA polymer, a phosphate group that is used to connect the ribose sugar molecules and a base adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or uracil (U) that are the carriers of information. The bases can form hydrogen bonds between cytosine and guanine, between adenine and uracil, and, between adenine and thymine (a base from DNA) (Source: Adapted from Wikipedia)













Figure 11: DNA is a polymer composed of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix carrying genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses. Each DNA single strand consists of a chain of nucleotides. Each nucleotide is build from a deoxyribose sugar that forms the backbone of the DNA polymer, a phosphate group that is used to connect the deoxyribose sugar molecules and a base adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T) that are the carriers of information. The bases form hydrogen bonds between cytosine and guanine, and, adenine and thymine to assemble single stranded DNA in double stranded DNA. (Source: Wikipedia)

title: Position of the course
text:
3.3 Life is Chemistry
“Life is Chemistry” because a cell consists of a complex network of chemical reactions that are connected to each other. Many feedback loops exist in this chemistry making it largely nonlinear. The feedback loops enable a cell to maintain in its regime or to switch from regime or attractor upon external and/or internal stimuli. An overview of most reactions in a living cell is given in Figure 12. You can zoom in on this map on http://biochemical-pathways.com/#/map/1.








Figure 12: Network of the most important reactions in a living cell (Source: Dr. Gerhard Michal, Roche)





In the remainder of this section we will introduce energy and catalysis in more detail, and we also give an intriguing example of how proteins play a role in the self-organisation of a cell.

3.3.1 Energy
“Life is Chemistry” because it uses chemical reactions to store and use energy. See the ATP-ADP system in Section 3.2.1.2


3.3.2 Catalysis
“Life is Chemistry” because most chemical reactions are catalyzed, i.e. initiated, promoted and made faster by proteins. The proteins facilitate the reaction without being used. The reactions would never take place if we would only mix the molecules at the concentrations that are typically occurring in a cell.
A catalyst is a chemical substance that helps a reaction to take place without being consumed. Proteins that are catalysts are also referred to as enzymes.
Enzymes are proteins that

initiate the reaction
speed up the reaction and
make sure that the outcome is always the same.

Loosely speaking they are

“fishing” certain molecules from the complex mixture in a cell,
which consists of thousands of chemical compounds generally at low concentrations,
through binding sites they can facilitate that these molecules (substrates) are getting close so that they can react and form a new compound.

These binding sites emerged from the unique 3D structure of the protein. In Figure 8 a schematic overview is given of the enzyme action of a protein.
In most cases enzymes work together in pathways, which consist of multiple chemical reactions for which (part of the) molecules produced in the previous reaction are used by another enzyme to facilitate the next reaction.
The Krebs cycle is a well known example. This pathway is the main source of energy for a cell through metabolising carbohydrates, lipids and/or proteins. The Krebs cycle is a cyclic pathway of multiple chemical reactions each catalyzed by another enzyme (see Figure 13 or the you tube movie https://www.youtube.com/embed/yk14dOOvwMk).
The Krebs cycle is also used to generate building blocks for constructing certain nucleotides and amino acids.








Figure 13: Krebs cycle, a cyclic pathway connecting multiple reactions that provide the main source of energy for our cells by metabolising carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. Each reaction is catalyzed by an enzyme (Source: Narayanese, Wikipedia)





We can end this section with a quote of De Duve (2002): “Any living organism is a reflection of its enzyme arsenal”.

title: Position of the course
text:
3.4 Life is Information
Our genetic information to build all our bio-molecules, which we inherit from our parents, is stored in our DNA. DNA is a hetero-polymer or a long chain of 4 different building blocks, nucleotides. So the genetic information is stored in an alphabet of 4 letters. This is adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T) for DNA.
It makes no physical or chemical difference what the identity of the next nucleotide is in the DNA chain. So our DNA can be seen as a coding system to store and pass genetic information from one generation to the next. Life is therefore also information and not only chemistry. It is absolutely mind blowing how variation in the sequence of this “four letter code” can lead to such a wealth of distinct characteristics and functions that can be observed between different specimens of the same species, and, even more so between different life forms.
In the remainder of this section we will focus on the flow of information in a cell in more detail.

3.4.1 The “central paradigm” of molecular biology
The “central paradigm” of molecular biology states that the sequence of nucleotides in DNA are first transcribed into RNA and then translated into proteins, see Figure 14.
Note, that some RNA molecules are also end products. Indeed RNA can also have a catalytic function, i.e. initiate and promote chemical reactions without being consumed.
A gene is the unit of genetic material, a DNA sequence that is encoding for the synthesis of a gene product, either a protein or a functional RNA.








Figure 14: Central paradigm of biology: a gene, a specific region in the DNA, is first transcribed into RNA and then into proteins. Note, that for RNA-genes the RNA molecule is the end product itself, which is referred to as non-coding RNA (ncRNA) (Source: Thomas Shafee, Wikipedia)






Figure 15 shows the process of transcription of a gene from DNA to RNA and the translation of RNA to proteins.

The transcription of DNA to RNA is initiated by opening the DNA double strand. Then a complementary RNA strand is synthesized by exploiting that A hybridizes to U (or T) and G to C through hydrogen bonds.
Once that the complementary RNA strand is made, it is further processed in the nucleus into messenger RNA (mRNA). The mRNA travels from the cell nucleus to the cell cytosol (cell liquid) where it is translated into proteins, and, where the majority of the reactions take place.
There mRNA is translated into proteins by ribosomes. In the ribosomes the mRNA is bound to transfer RNA (tRNA). tRNA can bind to the mRNA molecule if it has 3 consecutive nucleotides that are complementary to the triplet of the 3 consecutive nucleotides on the mRNA template that is lying in the ribosome.
The transfer RNA transports one specific amino-acid that is then incorporated in the protein that is being formed, which is the growing amino acid chain in Figure 15. The sequence of 3 consecutive nucleotides of DNA of a gene is therefore also called a codon because it encodes for a specific amino acid.
Upon incorporation, the ribosome shifts to the next triplet of the mRNA and the next transfer RNA is bound to it, and so on until a stop codon is reached and the protein is finished.









Figure 15: In the cell nucleus the DNA strand opens up and is transcribed into an RNA molecule. Upon processing, the messenger RNA (mRNA) travels from the nucleus to the cytosol where it is translated into proteins. The mRNA is the template that fits into a ribosome that has the function to bind transfer RNA molecules to the mRNA template. It does that by hybridising to a tRNA, which has a triplet of three nucleotides that are complementary to those of the mRNA template. The tRNAs have a amino acid on their tail, which is incorporated into a long chain of amino acids, the protein that is produced. If the amino acid is incorporated, the ribosome moves to the next triplet and the process happens all over with a new tRNA (Source: tokresources.org)





There are in total 64=4\(^3\) codons encoding for each of the 20 amino acids, and, for a start and a stop codon to initiate and stop the protein translation, respectively. Hence, there is a redundancy in the code, see Figure 16.








Figure 16: Codon table connecting triplets of nucleotids to amino acids (Source: Wikipedia)





We can learn an important message from the codon table:

There is no chemical necessity that explicitly connects the three nucleotides “CGG” to the amino acid arginine rather than to glutamine.
Nucleotides themselves do not seem to a have chemical connection to the amino acids they encode
Therefore we call it a code or information rather than just “genetic chemistry”

The code apparently evolved so that many mutations give rise to

synonymous codons (same amino acid) or
to incorporate amino acids that are similar

so that protein function is conserved.

DNA is thus the carrier of genetic information. However, RNA plays a more central role:

Messenger RNA brings the genetic information from the cell nucleus to the cell cytosol where they are translated into proteins and where most of the chemical reactions take place.
Ribozymes, i.e. catalytic RNA molecules, initiate and speed up particular reactions
Transfer RNA plays an crucial role in the translation of proteins
An RNA primer, i.e. a small RNA molecule, is essential to copy DNA
RNA also acts as carrier of genetic information, e.g. corona virus.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
In this chapter we introduce linear mixed models. We start from simple designs in which the response is measured repeatedly on the same experimental unit and analyse them first with a two-stage analysis: we summarise the data of each experimental unit and analyse the summaries. The linear mixed model does both stages in one step. The theory part follows Sections 4.1–4.8 of Ruppert et al. (2003): best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP), ML and REML estimation and inference.
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(Matrix)
library(QFeatures)
library(BiocFileCache)

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
1.1 Pseudo-replication: fish in tanks
Researchers want to assess the effect of three diets on the weight gain of fish. They have 12 tanks with the same number of fish. Each diet is randomly assigned to 4 tanks, and at the end of the experiment the weight gain of 6 fish in each tank is recorded.

fish <- data.frame(
  diet = factor(rep(1:3, each = 24)),
  tank = factor(rep(1:12, each = 6)),
  wtGain = c(
    8.8, 6.5, -1.1, 1.3, -0.6, 2.1,
    5.7, 4, -2.1, 2.3, 2.1, 7.5,
    -0.7, 11.2, -0.7, 11, 8.4, 5,
    3.4, 6.7, 11.3, 4, 2.6, 2.8,
    31, 15.7, 40.8, 33.8, 24.9, 31.4,
    10.5, 25.3, 18.6, 19.7, 20.7, 25.2,
    21.7, 15.9, 22.8, 21.5, 11.7, 17.7,
    38.6, 25.7, 32.3, 28.2, 28.6, 27.2,
    49.1, 39.7, 45.9, 48.6, 32.3, 60.2,
    61.7, 29.1, 49.1, 59.2, 45.8, 37.8,
    58.9, 43.2, 56.5, 47.5, 32.2, 62.4,
    59.4, 49.4, 42.3, 47, 48.4, 51.8))

ggplot(fish, aes(x = tank, y = wtGain, colour = diet)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()








Naive data analysis:

naiveFish <- lm(wtGain ~ diet, data = fish)
summary(naiveFish)$coef

             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  4.229167   1.528121  2.767560 7.244420e-03
diet2       20.333333   2.161090  9.408834 5.408316e-14
diet3       44.000000   2.161090 20.360099 6.933229e-31


Experimental units and observational units?

The diet is randomised to the tanks: the 12 tanks are the experimental units.
The weight gain is measured on the fish: the 72 fish are the observational units.
Fish in the same tank share the same environment (water quality, temperature, feeding, …): they are pseudo-replicates. Weighing more fish of the same tank does not give more independent tanks.


1.1.1 Two-stage analysis
The diet effect has to be assessed with the variability between the experimental units, the tanks. A simple and correct analysis therefore works in two stages:

Stage I: summarise the data of each experimental unit, here the average weight gain in each tank.
Stage II: analyse the summaries with an ordinary linear model: 4 tanks per diet.


stageIFish <- fish |>
  group_by(tank, diet) |>
  summarise(wtGain = mean(wtGain), .groups = "drop")
stageIFish

# A tibble: 12 × 3
   tank  diet  wtGain
   <fct> <fct>  <dbl>
 1 1     1       2.83
 2 2     1       3.25
 3 3     1       5.7 
 4 4     1       5.13
 5 5     2      29.6

 8 8     2      30.1 
 9 9     3      46.0 
10 10    3      47.1 
11 11    3      50.1 
12 12    3      49.7 

twoStageFish <- lm(wtGain ~ diet, data = stageIFish)
summary(twoStageFish)$coef

             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  4.229167   1.907782  2.216798 5.384469e-02
diet2       20.333333   2.698011  7.536416 3.554557e-05
diet3       44.000000   2.698011 16.308310 5.445651e-08


If we act as if the 72 fish are independent, the standard errors are too small: the analysis treats the 24 fish per diet as independent repeats, while there are only 4 independent tanks per diet.

summary(naiveFish)$coef

             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  4.229167   1.528121  2.767560 7.244420e-03
diet2       20.333333   2.161090  9.408834 5.408316e-14
diet3       44.000000   2.161090 20.360099 6.933229e-31


Note that we cannot correct for the tanks with a fixed tank effect as in a block design: once we know the tank, we also know the diet. The tank effects are aliased with the diet effects.

coef(lm(wtGain ~ diet + tank, data = fish))

(Intercept)       diet2       diet3       tank2       tank3       tank4 
  2.8333333  27.2666667  46.8833333   0.4166667   2.8666667   2.3000000 
      tank5       tank6       tank7       tank8       tank9      tank10 
 -0.5000000 -10.1000000 -11.5500000          NA  -3.7500000  -2.6000000 
     tank11      tank12 
  0.4000000          NA 




1.1.2 Linear mixed model
The two-stage analysis is easy, but it has drawbacks:

Information is lost when the data of a tank are summarised by a single number.
It is only valid when all Stage I summaries are equally precise, i.e. when the design is balanced. With unequal numbers of fish per tank, or missing values, the precision of the tank averages differs, and Stage II does not account for that.

A linear mixed model combines both stages into one model:
\[
\left\{\begin{array}{rcl}
y_{tk} &=& \beta_0 + \beta_{d(t)} + b_t + \epsilon_{tk}\\\\
b_t &\sim& N(0, \sigma^2_b), \\\\
\epsilon_{tk} &\sim& N(0, \sigma^2_\epsilon)
\end{array}\right.
\]
with \(y_{tk}\) the weight gain of fish \(k\) in tank \(t\), \(\beta_{d(t)}\) the effect of the diet of tank \(t\) and \(b_t\) a random effect for tank \(t\). (Note, that the random effects and errors are assumed to be independent.)

The diet effects are fixed effects: they are the parameters of interest.
The tank effects are random effects: the 12 tanks are a random sample of tanks, and we are not interested in the effect of these particular tanks. They only cost one extra parameter, the variance component \(\sigma^2_b\), the between-tank variance. \(\sigma^2_\epsilon\) is the within-tank variance.


lmmFish <- lmer(wtGain ~ diet + (1|tank), data = fish)
summary(lmmFish)

Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
Formula: wtGain ~ diet + (1 | tank)
   Data: fish

REML criterion at convergence: 481.9

Scaled residuals: 
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-2.60555 -0.45452 -0.05768  0.50128  1.97624 

Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 tank     (Intercept)  6.001   2.450   
 Residual             51.348   7.166   
Number of obs: 72, groups:  tank, 12

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)    4.229      1.908   2.217
diet2         20.333      2.698   7.536
diet3         44.000      2.698  16.308

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
      (Intr) diet2 
diet2 -0.707       
diet3 -0.707  0.500




1.1.3 Comparisons between analyses

rbind(
  wrong = summary(naiveFish)$coef["diet2", 1:3],
  twoStage = summary(twoStageFish)$coef["diet2", 1:3],
  mixed = summary(lmmFish)$coef["diet2", 1:3])

         Estimate Std. Error  t value
wrong    20.33333   2.161090 9.408834
twoStage 20.33333   2.698011 7.536416
mixed    20.33333   2.698011 7.536416


The two-stage analysis and the mixed model give identical estimates, standard errors and \(t\)-statistics. For a balanced design with \(m\) tanks per diet and \(n\) fish per tank, the variance of a diet mean is
\[
\text{var}\left[\bar y_{d}\right] = \frac{\sigma^2_b}{m} + \frac{\sigma^2_\epsilon}{mn}.
\]
The between-tank variance is only averaged over the \(m = 4\) independent tanks: weighing more fish per tank cannot reduce it. The mixed model accounts for both sources of variability.


1.1.4 Induced correlation
The random tank effect induces a correlation between fish of the same tank (\(k \neq k^\prime\)):
\[
\text{cov}\left[y_{tk}, y_{tk^\prime}\right] = \text{var}\left[b_t\right] = \sigma^2_b, \qquad
\text{corr}\left[y_{tk}, y_{tk^\prime}\right] = \frac{\sigma^2_b}{\sigma^2_b + \sigma^2_\epsilon}.
\]
Fish of different tanks remain independent. All fish of the same tank have the same variance \(\sigma^2_b + \sigma^2_\epsilon\) and the same correlation: this covariance structure is called compound symmetry. It is natural here, because the fish within a tank are exchangeable.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
1.2 Blocking: mouse T-cells
In the mouse T-cell experiment, regulatory (Treg) and conventional (Tconv) T-cells are purified from each of 4 mice. Here, the cell type varies within each mouse: the mouse is a block, a randomised complete block (RCB) design.

bfc <- BiocFileCache()
mouse <- readRDS(bfcrpath(bfc,"https://github.com/statOmics/msqrob2data/raw/refs/heads/main/dda/mouseTcell/qfeaturesRCB.rds"))

mouseProt <- data.frame(
  y = assay(mouse[["proteins"]])["B9EKR1", ],
  celltype = mouse$celltype,
  mouse = mouse$mouse)

ggplot(mouseProt, aes(x = celltype, y = y, group = mouse, colour = mouse)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal()








We compare

The two-stage analysis now summarises each mouse by the difference between its Treg and Tconv intensity (Stage I) and tests whether the average difference is zero (Stage II): a paired analysis.
ignoring the mouse effect
an RCB analysis with a fixed effect for mouse and
an RCB analysis with a random intercept for mouse.


stageIMouse <- mouseProt |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = celltype, values_from = y) |>
  mutate(diff = reg - con)
twoStageMouse <- lm(diff ~ 1, data = stageIMouse)

wrongMouse <- lm(y ~ celltype, data = mouseProt)
rcbMouse <- lm(y ~ celltype + mouse, data = mouseProt)
lmmMouse <- lmer(y ~ celltype + (1|mouse), data = mouseProt)

rbind(
  twoStage = summary(twoStageMouse)$coef[1, 1:3],
  wrong = summary(wrongMouse)$coef[2, 1:3],
  RCB = summary(rcbMouse)$coef[2, 1:3],
  mixed = summary(lmmMouse)$coef[2, 1:3])

          Estimate Std. Error    t value
twoStage 0.4507435 0.03788201 11.8986157
wrong    0.4507435 0.70334325  0.6408585
RCB      0.4507435 0.03788201 11.8986157
mixed    0.4507435 0.03788201 11.8986157



The two-stage (paired) analysis, the RCB analysis with a fixed block effect and the mixed model with a random block effect give identical results.
Ignoring the mouse effect inflates the standard error, because the between-mouse variability then ends up in the residual variance.

The cell type effect is estimated within each mouse. In the difference \(y_{\text{reg}, i} - y_{\text{con}, i} = \beta_\text{reg} + \epsilon_{\text{reg}, i} - \epsilon_{\text{con}, i}\) the mouse effect \(b_i\) cancels, so
\[
\text{var}\left[\bar y_\text{reg} - \bar y_\text{con}\right] = \frac{2\sigma^2_\epsilon}{m},
\]
which only involves the within-mouse variability. This is the advantage of blocking: the between-mouse variability is removed from the comparison.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
1.3 Summary










Design
Treatment varies
Unit of the random effect
Variance of treatment effect
Without random effect




Pseudo-replication
between units
experimental unit (tank, bio-repeat)
between + within unit
SE too small: liberal


Blocking (RCB)
within units
block (mouse)
within unit only
SE too large: conservative




In both designs the random intercept induces the correlation between observations of the same unit
The mixed model automatically uses the correct variance for the treatment effect.
In balanced designs it gives the same result as the two-stage analysis, but it also works for unbalanced designs.

Open issues:

Mixed model is problematic if random effect variance is estimated to be zero. Then data are treated as independent
Inference relies on asymptotic theory
Approximate inference in small samples is possible using approximations for the degrees of freedom
Unclear how to borrow strength across features for both random effect variance and error variance, and how to approximate the degrees of freedom in this context.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
1.4 Pseudo-replication in proteomics

Experiments with technical repeats for each biological repeat (see tutorials)
Inference at protein-level from peptide level data


1.4.1 Peptide level vs protein level analysis

Inference at protein level desired
Observational unit: precursors/PSM level
We perform two-stage analysis:

Summarisation
DA on protein summaries

Problem: theoretically invalid due to unbalanced data due to missingness
However, shown to work well in practice

With msqrob we started using peptide level models and explicitely addressed pseudo-replication:
\[
y_{ip} = \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}_i\boldsymbol{\beta}^\text{design} + \beta^\text{peptide}_p + b^\text{run}_i + \epsilon_{ip}
\]
protein-level:

\(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\text{design}\) \(\rightarrow\) DA estimates immediately estimated at the protein level from peptide level data.
\(b^\text{run} \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{run})\): random effect addressing pseudo-replication

peptide-level:

\(\beta^\text{peptide}_p\)
\(\epsilon_{ip} \sim N(0,\sigma^2_\epsilon)\)

\(\rightarrow\) Still available in msqrob2 via msqrobAggregate()
Problems:

Dissemination
No protein level summaries for plotting
Unclear which degrees of freedom to use
For some proteins random run effect variance is set at zero: then we act as if precursor/psm/peptide level data are independent
Computational complexity

See Sticker et al. 2020, 10.1074/mcp.RA119.001624 for comparison between peptide level and protein level models, showing that summarisation based approaches work fine when appropriate summarisation is used.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
2.1 Two-stage analysis

Stage I: fit a regression line for each pig \(i\) separately: \(y_{ij} = \beta_{0i} + \beta_{1i}\text{week}_j + \epsilon_{ij}\).
Stage II: analyse the pig-specific intercepts \(\hat\beta_{0i}\) and slopes \(\hat\beta_{1i}\), e.g. estimate the average slope and its standard error.


stageIPig <- pigs |>
  group_by(pig) |>
  summarise(
    intercept = coef(lm(weight ~ week))[1],
    slope = coef(lm(weight ~ week))[2])

ggplot(stageIPig, aes(x = slope)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  xlab("growth rate of a pig (kg/week)") +
  theme_minimal()







twoStagePig <- lm(slope ~ 1, data = stageIPig)
summary(twoStagePig)$coef

            Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 6.209896 0.09203821 67.47085 1.935218e-48


The standard error of the average growth rate is based on the variability of the growth rates between the 48 pigs, the experimental units.
The two-stage analysis has the same drawbacks as before, and some extra ones that are typical for longitudinal data:

Information is lost when the data of a pig are summarised by an intercept and a slope.
The precision of \(\hat\beta_{0i}\) and \(\hat\beta_{1i}\) depends on the number of measurements of pig \(i\) and on the time points at which they were taken. In practice, longitudinal data are often unbalanced, e.g. due to drop-out, and Stage II does not account for the differences in precision.
Stage II replaces the true \(\beta_{0i}\) and \(\beta_{1i}\) by estimates, which introduces extra variability that is not modelled.

title: Linear Mixed Models
section: 2.2 Linear mixed model with a random intercept and slope
text:
2.2 Linear mixed model with a random intercept and slope
The mixed model combines both stages:
\[
y_{ij} = (\beta_0 + b_{0i}) + (\beta_1 + b_{1i}) \text{week}_j + \epsilon_{ij}, \qquad
\left[\begin{array}{c} b_{0i} \\ b_{1i}\end{array}\right] \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{D}\right), \qquad
\epsilon_{ij} \text{ i.i.d. } N(0, \sigma^2_\epsilon),
\]
with

fixed effects \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\): the average intercept and growth rate in the population of pigs,
random effects \(b_{0i}\) and \(b_{1i}\): the deviation of the intercept and the growth rate of pig \(i\) from the population averages, independent between pigs,
variance components \(\sigma^2_\epsilon\) and \(\mathbf{D} = \left[\begin{array}{cc}\sigma^2_{b_0} & \sigma_{b_0b_1}\\ \sigma_{b_0b_1} & \sigma^2_{b_1}\end{array}\right]\).


lmmPigSlope <- lmer(weight ~ week + (week|pig), data = pigs)
summary(lmmPigSlope)

Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
Formula: weight ~ week + (week | pig)
   Data: pigs

REML criterion at convergence: 1740.9

Scaled residuals: 
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.6202 -0.5474  0.0150  0.5486  2.9939 

Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr  
 pig      (Intercept) 6.986    2.6432         
          week        0.380    0.6164   -0.06 
 Residual             1.597    1.2637         
Number of obs: 432, groups:  pig, 48

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept) 19.35561    0.40387   47.93
week         6.20990    0.09204   67.47

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
     (Intr)
week -0.132

rbind(
  `two-stage` = summary(twoStagePig)$coef[1, 1:2],
  `mixed model` = summary(lmmPigSlope)$coef["week", 1:2])

            Estimate Std. Error
two-stage   6.209896 0.09203821
mixed model 6.209896 0.09203775


The mixed model gives the same estimate and standard error of the average growth rate as the two-stage analysis, because the design is balanced: every pig is weighed in the same 9 weeks.
The random intercept and slope imply that the variance increases over time and that the correlation between two measurements of the same pig depends on when they were taken:
\[
\text{cov}\left[y_{ij}, y_{ij^\prime}\right] =
\left[\begin{array}{cc} 1 & \text{week}_j\end{array}\right] \mathbf{D} \left[\begin{array}{c} 1 \\ \text{week}_{j^\prime}\end{array}\right] + \sigma^2_\epsilon \delta_{jj^\prime}
= \sigma^2_{b_0} + \sigma_{b_0b_1}(\text{week}_j + \text{week}_{j^\prime}) + \sigma^2_{b_1}\text{week}_j\text{week}_{j^\prime} + \sigma^2_\epsilon\delta_{jj^\prime},
\]
with \(\delta_{jj^\prime} = 1\) if \(j = j^\prime\) and 0 otherwise.

title: Linear Mixed Models
section: 2.3 Why not a random intercept only?
text:
2.3 Why not a random intercept only?
We compare the mixed model with three simpler models:

Ignore the pigs: \(y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{week}_j + \epsilon_{ij}\).
A fixed intercept \(\alpha_i\) for each pig, as in a block design: \(y_{ij} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 \text{week}_j + \epsilon_{ij}\).
A random intercept for each pig: \(y_{ij} = \beta_0 + b_i + \beta_1 \text{week}_j + \epsilon_{ij}\), \(b_i \text{ i.i.d. } N(0, \sigma^2_b)\).


lmOLS <- lm(weight ~ week, data = pigs)
lmFixed <- lm(weight ~ pig + week, data = pigs)
lmmPig <- lmer(weight ~ week + (1|pig), data = pigs)

rbind(
  `model 1: ignore pigs` = summary(lmOLS)$coef["week", 1:2],
  `model 2: fixed pig intercepts` = summary(lmFixed)$coef["week", 1:2],
  `model 3: random intercept` = summary(lmmPig)$coef["week", 1:2],
  `two-stage: slope per pig` = summary(twoStagePig)$coef[1, 1:2],
  `random intercept + slope` = summary(lmmPigSlope)$coef["week", 1:2])

                              Estimate Std. Error
model 1: ignore pigs          6.209896 0.08184093
model 2: fixed pig intercepts 6.209896 0.03906329
model 3: random intercept     6.209896 0.03906329
two-stage: slope per pig      6.209896 0.09203821
random intercept + slope      6.209896 0.09203775



Model 2 (a block analysis with a fixed effect for each pig) and model 3 (random intercept) give a standard error that is less than half as large as the two-stage analysis: they are too liberal.
They remove the differences in level between pigs, but assume that all pigs grow at the same rate.
The variation of the growth rates between pigs (the pig \(\times\) week interaction) then ends up in the residuals, and the slope is tested against the within-pig variability only.
This is again a form of pseudo-replication: the 9 measurements of a pig are treated as 9 independent pieces of information on the growth rate in the population.
Model 2 also uses 49 parameters, and its intercepts only describe these 48 pigs.
Model 1 is closer to the correct standard error, but only because two errors partly cancel each other out.

Whenever an effect is assessed repeatedly within an experimental unit, its variation between the units has to be part of its standard error!

In the mouse T-cell example there is only one observation per mouse and cell type
so the mouse \(\times\) cell type interaction automatically ends up in the residual and the block analysis is correct.
If each mouse were measured in several MS-runs per cell type, a random effect for mouse \(\times\) cell type, (1|mouse) + (1|mouse:celltype), would be needed.


2.3.1 Residuals of model 1
The residuals of model 1, which ignores the pigs, show the correlation structure in the data.

pigs$resOLS <- residuals(lmOLS)

ggplot(pigs, aes(x = week, y = resOLS, group = pig)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ylab("residual model 1") +
  theme_minimal()







pigs |>
  mutate(pig = fct_reorder(pig, resOLS, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pig, y = resOLS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  xlab("pig (ordered by median residual)") +
  ylab("residual model 1") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())







resWide <- pigs |>
  dplyr::select(pig, week, resOLS) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = week, values_from = resOLS)


A pig that is heavier than average in week 1 tends to remain heavier than average in all other weeks: the residuals of the same pig are strongly correlated.
The residuals of different pigs are centred around very different values: for many pigs the whole box lies above or below zero, and the boxes of the lightest and heaviest pigs do not overlap.
The residuals fan out: their variance increases over time.



2.3.2 Residuals of model 2
The block analysis of model 2 removes the differences in level between the pigs. Do its residuals still show a correlation structure? We colour the pigs according to their growth rate from Stage I of the two-stage analysis.

pigs$resFixed <- residuals(lmFixed)
pigs <- pigs |>
  left_join(stageIPig |> dplyr::select(pig, slope), by = "pig")

ggplot(pigs, aes(x = week, y = resFixed, group = pig, colour = slope)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "growth rate\n(kg/week)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  ylab("residual model 2") +
  theme_minimal()







pigs |>
  mutate(pig = fct_reorder(pig, slope)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pig, y = resFixed)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  xlab("pig (ordered by growth rate)") +
  ylab("residual model 2") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())









All boxes are now centred around zero: the fixed pig effects remove the differences in level between the pigs.
But the residuals of a pig are not random noise around zero: pigs that grow faster than average have negative residuals in the early weeks and positive residuals in the late weeks, and vice versa for pigs that grow slowly.
The residuals of a pig thus follow a line whose slope is the deviation of its growth rate from the average growth rate: the pig \(\times\) week interaction ends up in the residuals.
The residual variance is smallest in the middle weeks and largest in the first and last weeks.


resFixedWide <- pigs |>
  dplyr::select(pig, week, resFixed) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = week, values_from = resFixed)

corFixed <- cor(resFixedWide[, -1])

tibble(
  week1 = rep(1:9, times = 9),
  week2 = rep(1:9, each = 9),
  correlation = as.vector(corFixed)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week1, y = week2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  coord_equal() +
  xlab("week") +
  ylab("week") +
  theme_minimal()









Residuals of the same pig in nearby weeks are positively correlated, residuals in early and late weeks are negatively correlated.
This is exactly the pattern induced by pig-specific slopes, and it violates the independence assumption of model 2.
Model 2 treats the 9 residuals of a pig as independent, so the variation of the growth rates between pigs is used as if it were within-pig noise, while the growth rate is assessed within each pig. Its standard error for the average growth rate is therefore too small.

Note that the within-pig error is not underestimated by model 2: its residual standard deviation is even larger than that of the random slope model.

c(`model 2` = sigma(lmFixed), `random intercept + slope` = sigma(lmmPigSlope))

                 model 2 random intercept + slope 
                2.096356                 1.263658 


The problem is that model 2 uses the wrong error term to assess the growth rate. We can see this by splitting the residual sum of squares of model 2 into two parts by adding the pig \(\times\) week interaction, i.e. a separate slope for each pig:

lmPigSlopes <- lm(weight ~ pig + week + pig:week, data = pigs)
ssTab <- anova(lmFixed, lmPigSlopes)

decomp <- tibble(
  source = c(
    "differences in slope between pigs (pig x week)",
    "scatter around the line of each pig",
    "residual model 2 (pooled)"),
  SS = c(ssTab$`Sum of Sq`[2], ssTab$RSS[2], ssTab$RSS[1]),
  df = c(ssTab$Df[2], ssTab$Res.Df[2], ssTab$Res.Df[1])) |>
  mutate(MS = SS / df)
decomp

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  source                                            SS    df    MS
  <chr>                                          <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 differences in slope between pigs (pig x week) 1147.    47 24.4 
2 scatter around the line of each pig             537.   336  1.60
3 residual model 2 (pooled)                      1683.   383  4.39



The growth rate is assessed within each pig, so its standard error has to be based on how much the growth rates vary between the pigs: the first row, with 47 degrees of freedom.
Model 2 does not know about this split: it pools the slope differences with the scatter around the pig-specific lines and divides by 383 instead of 47 degrees of freedom.
Because there are many more degrees of freedom for the scatter around the lines than for the differences between pigs, the variability of the growth rates is diluted and the error term becomes much too small.
The mean square of the second row, 1.6, is an estimate of the pure within-pig error variance, close to \(\hat\sigma^2_\epsilon =\) 1.6 of the random slope model.

With \(n = 48\) pigs and \(S_{xx} = \sum_{j=1}^9 (\text{week}_j - \overline{\text{week}})^2 = 60\), the standard error of the average growth rate is \(\sqrt{\text{MS}/(n S_{xx})}\):

Sxx <- sum((1:9 - mean(1:9))^2)
n <- nlevels(pigs$pig)
c(`MS pig x week (correct)` = sqrt(decomp$MS[1] / (n * Sxx)),
  `MS pooled (model 2)` = sqrt(decomp$MS[3] / (n * Sxx)))

MS pig x week (correct)     MS pooled (model 2) 
             0.09203821              0.03906329 



With the mean square of the pig \(\times\) week interaction we recover the standard error of the two-stage analysis and of the random slope model.
With the pooled mean square we recover the much too small standard error of model 2.
This is the same reasoning as in a split-plot ANOVA: an effect has to be tested against the variability of the units at which it varies.

The random intercept model (model 3) implies compound symmetry:

all measurements of the same pig have the same variance \[\sigma^2_b + \sigma^2_\epsilon\] and
the same correlation whatever the time between them: \[\sigma^2_b/(\sigma^2_b + \sigma^2_\epsilon).\]
That is natural for fish in a tank or MS-runs of a bio-repeat, but not for repeated measurements over time when subjects grow at different rates.

With a random intercept and slope, the correlation between two measurements of the same pig depends on the weeks at which they were taken:
\[
\text{corr}\left[y_{ij}, y_{ij^\prime}\right] = \frac{\sigma^2_{b_0} + \sigma_{b_0b_1}(\text{week}_j + \text{week}_{j^\prime}) + \sigma^2_{b_1}\text{week}_j\text{week}_{j^\prime}}{\sqrt{v_j v_{j^\prime}}}
\]
\[
v_j = \sigma^2_{b_0} + 2\sigma_{b_0b_1}\text{week}_j + \sigma^2_{b_1}\text{week}_j^2 + \sigma^2_\epsilon.
\]
We compare the observed correlations with the correlations implied by both models.

# implied correlation matrix of the 9 measurements of a pig
impliedCor <- function(fit, Zi) {
  D <- bdiag(VarCorr(fit)) |> as.matrix()
  Vi <- Zi %*% D %*% t(Zi) + diag(nrow(Zi)) * sigma(fit)^2
  cov2cor(Vi)
}

corMats <- list(
  observed = cor(resWide[, -1]),
  `random intercept` = impliedCor(lmmPig, matrix(1, 9, 1)),
  `random intercept + slope` = impliedCor(lmmPigSlope, cbind(1, 1:9)))

corMats |> 
  map(\(corMat) tibble(
    week1 = rep(1:9, times = 9), 
    week2 = rep(1:9, each = 9), 
    correlation = as.vector(corMat))) |> 
  bind_rows(.id = "matrix") |> 
  mutate(matrix = factor(matrix, levels = names(corMats))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week1, y = week2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2)), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  coord_equal() +
  facet_wrap(~ matrix) +
  xlab("week") +
  ylab("week") +
  theme_minimal()









The random intercept model implies the same correlation for all pairs of weeks.
In the observed data the correlation decreases with the time between the measurements, and the random intercept and slope model captures this pattern. In the early weeks the weight of a pig is mainly determined by its random intercept, in the later weeks by its random slope, whose contribution grows with time. Hence, measurements in the later weeks are more strongly correlated than measurements in the early weeks.
Measurements in consecutive weeks are still somewhat more correlated than implied by the random slope model, especially in the early weeks. Growth curves are not exactly linear for every pig, which could be modelled with a serial correlation structure or a random quadratic term. We do not pursue this here.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
4.1 Best prediction
Suppose we observe \(y = v + \epsilon\) with \(v \sim N(0, 1)\) and \(\epsilon \sim N(0, 4)\) independent. What is the best guess for the unobserved \(v\)?
The best predictor minimises \(E\left[(\tilde v - v)^2\right]\) and equals \(\tilde v = E\left[v \vert y\right]\).
Regression view. Because \(v\) and \(y\) are jointly normal, \(E\left[v \vert y\right]\) is the regression line of \(v\) on \(y\):
\[
E\left[v \vert y\right] = E\left[v\right] + \frac{\text{cov}\left[v, y\right]}{\text{var}\left[y\right]}\{y - E\left[y\right]\},
\]
with \(\text{cov}\left[v, y\right] = \text{cov}\left[v, v + \epsilon\right] = \text{var}\left[v\right] = 1\), \(\text{var}\left[y\right] = \text{var}\left[v\right] + \text{var}\left[\epsilon\right] = 5\) and \(E\left[v\right] = E\left[y\right] = 0\). Hence
\[
\tilde v = E\left[v \vert y\right] = \frac{y}{5}.
\]
Only 1/5 of the variability in \(y\) comes from \(v\), so we only keep 1/5 of what we observe: the prediction is a shrunken version of \(y\).
We can see this by simulation: the regression of \(v\) on \(y\) has slope 1/5, not 1.

set.seed(1)
sim <- tibble(
  v = rnorm(5000, mean = 0, sd = 1),
  y = v + rnorm(5000, mean = 0, sd = 2))

coef(lm(v ~ y, data = sim))

(Intercept)           y 
0.001607151 0.208870743 

ggplot(sim, aes(x = y, y = v)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_abline(
    data = tibble(slope = c(1, 1/5), line = c("v = y", "v = y/5")),
    aes(intercept = 0, slope = slope, linetype = line)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = NULL, values = c("dashed", "solid")) +
  theme_minimal()








Precision-weighted view. We have two sources of information on \(v\):

the prior mean \(E\left[v\right] = 0\), with precision \(1/\text{var}\left[v\right] = 1\),
the observation \(y\), with precision \(1/\text{var}\left[\epsilon\right] = 1/4\).

The best predictor is their precision-weighted average:
\[
\tilde v = \frac{1 \times 0 + \frac{1}{4} \times y}{1 + \frac{1}{4}} = \frac{y}{5}.
\]
The noisier the observation, the lower its precision and the stronger the shrinkage towards the mean of \(v\).

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
4.2 Fish tanks
For the random intercept model of the fish, the best predictor of the effect of tank \(t\) is
\[
\tilde b_t = \frac{n \sigma^2_b}{\sigma^2_\epsilon + n \sigma^2_b}(\bar y_{t\cdot} - \beta_0 - \beta_{d(t)}),
\]
i.e. the deviation of the tank average from its diet mean, shrunken towards 0. This is again a precision-weighted average: the tank average has precision \(n/\sigma^2_\epsilon\) and the prior mean 0 of \(b_t\) has precision \(1/\sigma^2_b\), so
\[
\tilde b_t = \frac{\frac{1}{\sigma^2_b} \times 0 + \frac{n}{\sigma^2_\epsilon}(\bar y_{t\cdot} - \beta_0 - \beta_{d(t)})}{\frac{1}{\sigma^2_b} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2_\epsilon}}.
\]
The shrinkage is strong when there are few observations per unit or when \(\sigma^2_\epsilon\) is large compared to \(\sigma^2_b\).

vcFish <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(lmmFish))
sigma2b <- vcFish$vcov[vcFish$grp == "tank"]
sigma2EpsFish <- vcFish$vcov[vcFish$grp == "Residual"]
nFish <- 6

shrinkFish <- nFish * sigma2b / (sigma2EpsFish + nFish * sigma2b)
shrinkFish

[1] 0.4121706

dietMeans <- predict(lmmFish, newdata = stageIFish, re.form = NA)
tankEffects <- tibble(
  tank = stageIFish$tank,
  `tank average - diet mean` = stageIFish$wtGain - dietMeans,
  byHand = shrinkFish * `tank average - diet mean`,
  lme4 = ranef(lmmFish)$tank[, 1])
tankEffects

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
4.3 Pig-specific growth curves
For the pigs, the mixed model predicts a pig-specific intercept \(\beta_0 + b_{0i}\) and growth rate \(\beta_1 + b_{1i}\). They are shrunken towards the population averages compared to the Stage I regression lines of each pig.

blupPig <- coef(lmmPigSlope)$pig |>
  rownames_to_column("pig")

stageIPig |>
  mutate(pig = as.character(pig)) |>
  left_join(blupPig, by = "pig") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = slope, y = week)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fixef(lmmPigSlope)["week"], colour = "grey") +
  xlab("growth rate Stage I regression") +
  ylab("growth rate mixed model (BLUP)") +
  theme_minimal()








The growth rates are shrunken towards the average growth rate (grey line), but only mildly: each pig has 9 measurements and the within-pig variance is small compared to the variance of the growth rates between pigs.

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
6.1 Fixed effects: generalised least squares
Write \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^*\) with \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^* = \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{b} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) and \(\text{var}\left[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^*\right] = \mathbf{V}\). For known \(\mathbf{V}\), the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is the generalised least squares estimator
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{y}.
\]

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
6.2 Random effects: BLUP
For known \(\boldsymbol\beta\), the best predictor of \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(E\left[\mathbf{b} \vert \mathbf{y}\right] = \mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)\). The best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) is this best predictor in which the unknown \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is replaced by its GLS estimate \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\):
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}).
\]

Vinv <- solve(V)
betaTilde <- solve(t(X) %*% Vinv %*% X, t(X) %*% Vinv %*% y)
uTilde <- G %*% t(Z) %*% Vinv %*% (y - X %*% betaTilde)

cbind(GLS = betaTilde[, 1], lme4 = fixef(lmmPigSlope))

                  GLS      lme4
(Intercept) 19.355613 19.355613
week         6.209896  6.209896

head(cbind(
  intercept = uTilde[1:m, 1],
  slope = uTilde[m + 1:m, 1],
  ranef(lmmPigSlope)$pig))

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
6.3 BLUP as penalised least squares
Henderson’s justification assumes \(\mathbf{y} \vert \mathbf{b} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{R})\) and \(\mathbf{b} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) and maximises the joint likelihood of \((\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{b})\), which amounts to minimising
\[
(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta - \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{b})^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta - \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{b}) + \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{G}^{-1}\mathbf{b}.
\]
This is generalised least squares with a ridge penalty on the random effects only. With \(\mathbf{C} = [\mathbf{X}\ \mathbf{Z}]\) and \(\mathbf{B} = \text{blockdiag}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G}^{-1})\) the solution is
\[
\left[\begin{array}{c}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\\ \tilde{\mathbf{b}}\end{array}\right] =
(\mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{C} + \mathbf{B})^{-1}\mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{y}.
\]

C <- cbind(X, Z)
B <- bdiag(matrix(0, 2, 2), solve(G)) |> as.matrix()
Rinv <- diag(1 / sigma2Eps, n)
A <- solve(t(C) %*% Rinv %*% C + B)
ridge <- A %*% t(C) %*% Rinv %*% y

head(cbind(ridge = ridge[, 1], GLS_BLUP = c(betaTilde, uTilde)))

                 ridge   GLS_BLUP
(Intercept) 19.3556134 19.3556134
week         6.2098958  6.2098958
pig1         0.2402199  0.2402199
pig2        -1.5915118 -1.5915118
pig3        -3.5374496 -3.5374496
pig4         1.9744827  1.9744827


Setting the derivative of Henderson’s criterion with respect to \(\mathbf{b}\) to zero shows where the shrinkage comes from. With \(\mathbf{R} = \sigma^2_\epsilon\mathbf{I}\):
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{b}} = \left(\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z} + \sigma^2_\epsilon\mathbf{G}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{Z}^T(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}),
\]
while least squares with \(\mathbf{b}\) as fixed effects would give \((\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}^T(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})\): the Stage I regression line of each pig minus the population line. The term \(\sigma^2_\epsilon\mathbf{G}^{-1}\) shrinks the random effects towards zero. For a random intercept model with \(n\) observations per unit, \(\mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Z} = n\mathbf{I}\) and \(\mathbf{G} = \sigma^2_b \mathbf{I}\), which gives the shrinkage factor \(n\sigma^2_b/(n\sigma^2_b + \sigma^2_\epsilon)\) of the fish tanks.

res <- y - X %*% betaTilde
uShrunk <- solve(t(Z) %*% Z + sigma2Eps * solve(G), t(Z) %*% res)
uLS <- solve(t(Z) %*% Z, t(Z) %*% res)

# random slopes

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
6.4 Variance components: ML and REML
The variance components in \(\mathbf{V}\) are estimated by maximising a likelihood of the marginal model \(\mathbf{y} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta, \mathbf{V})\).

ML maximises the profile log-likelihood \[
\ell_P(\mathbf{V}) = -\frac{1}{2}\left\{\log\vert\mathbf{V}\vert + (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}) + n\log(2\pi)\right\}.
\]
REML (restricted maximum likelihood) maximises the likelihood of linear combinations of \(\mathbf{y}\) that do not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\): \[
\ell_R(\mathbf{V}) = \ell_P(\mathbf{V}) - \frac{1}{2}\log\vert\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\vert.
\]

What are linear combinations that do not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\)? Take \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y}\) with \(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}\). Then
\[
\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \mathbf{A}^T(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{b} + \boldsymbol\epsilon) = \mathbf{A}^T(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{b} + \boldsymbol\epsilon) \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{V}\mathbf{A}),
\]
so the fixed effects drop out and the distribution of \(\mathbf{w}\) only depends on the variance components. There are only \(n - p\) linearly independent combinations of this kind, the so-called error contrasts, with \(p\) the number of fixed effects. You can think of \(\mathbf{w}\) as the residuals after fitting the fixed effects with least squares, \(\{\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\}\mathbf{y}\): their distribution does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\). REML maximises the likelihood of \(\mathbf{w}\), which results in \(\ell_R(\mathbf{V})\) above whatever choice of \(\mathbf{A}\) is made.
ML estimates the variance components as if \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) were the true \(\boldsymbol\beta\), while REML only uses the information that is left after removing the fixed effects. Hence, REML accounts for the degrees of freedom used to estimate the fixed effects. For a sample \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\): \(\hat\sigma^2_\text{ML} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (X_i - \bar X)^2\) while \(\hat\sigma^2_\text{REML} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (X_i - \bar X)^2\). REML is based on the contrasts \(X_i - \bar X\), which do not depend on \(\mu\), and only \(n - 1\) of them are linearly independent because they sum to zero. For small samples REML is preferred; for large samples both give similar results. REML is the default in lmer.

lmmPigSlopeML <- lmer(weight ~ week + (week|pig), data = pigs, REML = FALSE)
tibble(
  component = c("var intercept", "var slope", "cov intercept slope", "var residual"),
  ML = as.data.frame(VarCorr(lmmPigSlopeML))$vcov,
  REML = as.data.frame(VarCorr(lmmPigSlope))$vcov)

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
6.5 Estimated BLUP
In practice \(\mathbf{G}\) and \(\mathbf{R}\) are unknown and replaced by their (RE)ML estimates:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^T\hat{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\hat{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}\mathbf{y}, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \hat{\mathbf{G}}\mathbf{Z}^T\hat{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}).
\]
These are estimated BLUPs (EBLUPs). They are what fixef() and ranef() return (and what we computed above, because we plugged in the REML estimates).

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
7.1 Standard errors
\[
\text{var}\left[\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\right] = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\]
and the standard errors are obtained by plugging in \(\hat{\mathbf{V}}\).

cbind(byHand = sqrt(diag(solve(t(X) %*% Vinv %*% X))),
      lme4 = summary(lmmPigSlope)$coef[, 2])

                byHand       lme4
(Intercept) 0.40386734 0.40386734
week        0.09203775 0.09203775


This ignores the uncertainty in the estimated variance components. That is negligible in large samples but not in small experiments. Small-sample corrections approximate the degrees of freedom of the resulting \(t\)-statistics, e.g. Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger (packages lmerTest and pbkrtest). The precision of the BLUPs follows from \(\text{var}\left[\begin{array}{c}\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\\ \tilde{\mathbf{b}} - \mathbf{b}\end{array}\right] = (\mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{C} + \mathbf{B})^{-1}\).

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
7.2 Tests for fixed effects

Wald test: \(z = \hat\beta_k/\text{se}(\hat\beta_k) \approx N(0, 1)\) under \(H_0: \beta_k = 0\).
Likelihood ratio test (LRT): \(-2\log \text{LR} = -2\{\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_0) - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\} \approx \chi^2_\nu\), with \(\nu\) the difference in the number of parameters.

Use ML, not REML, to compare models with different fixed effects: the restricted likelihood is the likelihood of the residuals after fitting the fixed effects, so it is not comparable across different fixed effects models.

lmmPigSlopeML0 <- lmer(weight ~ 1 + (week|pig), data = pigs, REML = FALSE)
anova(lmmPigSlopeML0, lmmPigSlopeML)

Data: pigs
Models:
lmmPigSlopeML0: weight ~ 1 + (week | pig)
lmmPigSlopeML: weight ~ week + (week | pig)
               npar    AIC    BIC  logLik -2*log(L)  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
lmmPigSlopeML0    5 1967.9 1988.3 -978.97    1957.9                         
lmmPigSlopeML     6 1749.9 1774.3 -868.96    1737.9 220.01  1  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: Linear Mixed Models
text:
7.3 Testing a variance component
Is there between-unit variability, e.g. \(H_0: \sigma^2_b = 0\) versus \(H_1: \sigma^2_b > 0\) in the random intercept model?
Under \(H_0\) the parameter is on the boundary of its parameter space \([0, \infty)\), so the classical \(\chi^2_1\) approximation of the LRT does not hold. When the number of independent subjects is large, \(-2\log\text{LR}\) follows a 50:50 mixture of a point mass at zero and a \(\chi^2_1\) distribution (Self and Liang 1987): in half of the datasets \(\hat\sigma^2_b\) = 0. Using \(\chi^2_1\) therefore gives p-values that are twice too large.
We can check this by simulating data under \(H_0\), i.e. from the fitted model 1 that ignores the pigs, and computing the LRT for each simulated dataset.

set.seed(1)
lrtNull <- replicate(200, {
  ySim <- simulate(lmOLS)[, 1]
  ml1 <- lmer(ySim ~ week + (1|pig), data = pigs, REML = FALSE)
  ml0 <- lm(ySim ~ week, data = pigs)
  max(0, 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(ml1)) - as.numeric(logLik(ml0))))
})

mean(lrtNull < 1e-6) # proportion of LRT statistics equal to zero

[1] 0.595

ggplot(data.frame(lrt = lrtNull[lrtNull > 1e-6]), aes(x = lrt)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20) +
  geom_function(fun = dchisq, args = list(df = 1)) +
  xlim(0, 8) +
  ggtitle("Nonzero LRT statistics under H0 vs chi-square 1") +
  theme_minimal()








About half of the simulated LRT statistics are zero; in finite samples this proportion is typically somewhat larger than 1/2 (Ruppert et al. 2003), so the 50:50 mixture is slightly conservative.
To test whether we need a random slope, we compare the random intercept model with the random intercept and slope model. Under \(H_0\) the variance of the random slope is zero and the covariance between the random intercept and slope then also vanishes. The LRT then follows a 50:50 mixture of a \(\chi^2_1\) and a \(\chi^2_2\) distribution. Both models have the same fixed effects, so we can also use their restricted likelihoods.

anova(lmmPig, lmmPigSlope, refit = FALSE)

Data: pigs
Models:
lmmPig: weight ~ week + (1 | pig)
lmmPigSlope: weight ~ week + (week | pig)
            npar    AIC    BIC   logLik -2*log(L)  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
lmmPig         4 2041.8 2058.1 -1016.90    2033.8                         
lmmPigSlope    6 1752.9 1777.3  -870.44    1740.9 292.93  2  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

lrtSlope <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(lmmPigSlope)) - as.numeric(logLik(lmmPig)))
c(LRT = lrtSlope,
  pval = 0.5 * pchisq(lrtSlope, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) +
    0.5 * pchisq(lrtSlope, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE))

         LRT         pval 
2.929256e+02 1.290343e-64 


The random slope is clearly needed. With few subjects or many observations per subject the mixture approximations are also inaccurate. In those cases the null distribution is best obtained by simulation, as above (parametric bootstrap).

title: Recap general linear model
text:
5.1 Scalar form

Consider a vector of predictors \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)^T\) and
a real-valued response \(Y\)
then the linear regression model can be written as \[
Y=f(\mathbf{x}) +\epsilon=\beta_0+\sum\limits_{j=1}^p x_j\beta_j + \epsilon
\] with i.i.d. \(\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\)

title: Recap general linear model
text:
5.2 Matrix form

\(n\) observations \((\mathbf{x}_1,y_1) \ldots (\mathbf{x}_n,y_n)\)
Regression in matrix notation \[\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X\beta} + \mathbf{\epsilon}\] with \(\mathbf{Y}=\left[\begin{array}{c}y_1\\ \vdots\\y_n\end{array}\right]\), \(\mathbf{X}=\left[\begin{array}{cccc} 1&x_{11}&\ldots&x_{1p}\\
\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\
1&x_{n1}&\ldots&x_{np}
\end{array}\right]\), \(\mathbf{\beta}=\left[\begin{array}{c}\beta_0\\ \vdots\\ \beta_p\end{array}\right]\) and \(\mathbf{\epsilon}=\left[\begin{array}{c} \epsilon_1 \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_n\end{array}\right]\)

title: Recap general linear model
text:
5.3 Least Squares (LS)

Minimize the residual sum of squares \[\begin{eqnarray*}
RSS(\mathbf{\beta})&=&\sum\limits_{i=1}^n e^2_i\\
&=&\sum\limits_{i=1}^n \left(y_i-\beta_0-\sum\limits_{j=1}^p x_{ij}\beta_j\right)^2
\end{eqnarray*}\]
or in matrix notation \[\begin{eqnarray*}
RSS(\mathbf{\beta})&=&(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta})^T(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta})\\
&=&\Vert \mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta}\Vert^2_2
\end{eqnarray*}\] with the \(L_2\)-norm of a \(p\)-dim. vector \(v\) \(\Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert=\sqrt{v_1^2+\ldots+v_p^2}\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}=\text{argmin}_\beta \Vert \mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta}\Vert^2_2\)



5.3.1 Minimize RSS
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \mathbf{\beta}}&=&\mathbf{0}\\\\
\frac{(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta})^T(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta})}{\partial \mathbf{\beta}}&=&\mathbf{0}\\\\
-2\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X\beta})&=&\mathbf{0}\\\\
\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X\beta}&=&\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}\\\\
\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}
\end{array}
\]



5.3.2 Geometric Interpretation

Toy dataset
We will illustrate this on a toy dataset

library(tidyverse)
data <- data.frame(x=1:3,y=c(1,2,2))
data

  x y
1 1 1
2 2 2
3 3 2




Matrix form for toy dataset
We can also write this in matrix form
\[
\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}
\]
with
\[
\mathbf{Y}=\left[
\begin{array}{c}
1\\
2\\
2\\
\end{array}\right],
\quad
\mathbf{X}= \left[
\begin{array}{cc}
1&1\\
1&2\\
1&3\\
\end{array}
\right],
\quad \boldsymbol{\beta} = \left[
\begin{array}{c}
\beta_0\\
\beta_1\\
\end{array}
\right]
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
\epsilon_1\\
\epsilon_2\\
\epsilon_3
\end{array}
\right]
\]


Classical interpretation
Model fit and predictions based on the toy dataset

data$yhat <- lm1$fitted

  ggplot(aes(x,y)) +
  geom_point() +
  ylim(0,4) +
  xlim(0,4) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", fullrange = TRUE) +
  geom_point(aes(x=x, y =yhat), pch = 2, size = 3, color = "red") +

-Inf












5.3.3 Projection
There is also another picture to regression:

Instead of plotting each observation \(i= 1 \ldots n\) as a data-point in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) with dimensions \(1 \ldots p\) for every variable/feature that is recorded for each observation
We can also plot \(\mathbf{Y}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}\) and each column of \(\mathbf{X}\): \(\mathbf{X}_j\) with \(j=1 \ldots p\) as a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with dimensions \(1 \ldots n\) for every observation.
In this representation linear regression can be interpreted as a projection of the vector \(\mathbf{Y}\) onto the subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) that is spanned by the vectors for the predictors \(\mathbf{X}_1 \ldots \mathbf{X}_p\).
The space \(\mathbf{X}_1 \ldots \mathbf{X}_p\) is also referred to as the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\), the space that consists of all linear combinations of the vectors of the predictors or columns \(\mathbf{X}_1 \ldots \mathbf{X}_p\).


Intermezzo: Projection of vector on X and Y axis
\[
\mathbf{e}=\left[\begin{array}{c} e_1\\e_2\end{array}\right], \mathbf{u}_1 =  \left[\begin{array}{c} 1\\0\end{array}\right], \mathbf{u}_2 =  \left[\begin{array}{c} 0\\1\end{array}\right]
\]

ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.










Projection of error on x-axis

\[\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathbf{u}_1^T \mathbf{e} &=& \Vert \mathbf{u}_1\Vert_2  \Vert \mathbf{e}_1\Vert_2 \cos <\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{e}_1>\\
&=&\left[\begin{array}{cc} 1&0\end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{c} e_1\\e_2\end{array}\right]\\ &=& 1\times e_1 + 0 \times e_2 \\
&=& e_1\\
\end{eqnarray*}\]

Projection of error on y-axis

\[\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathbf{u}_2^T \mathbf{e} &=& \left[\begin{array}{cc} 0&1\end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{c} e_1\\e_2\end{array}\right]\\ &=& 0\times e_1 + 1 \times e_2 \\
&=& e_2
\end{eqnarray*}\]

Projection of error on itself

\[\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathbf{e}^T \mathbf{e} &=&\left[\begin{array}{cc} e_1&e_2\end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{c} e_1\\e_2\end{array}\right]\\
&=&e_1^2+e_2^2\\
&=&\Vert e \Vert^2_2 \rightarrow \text{ Pythagorean theorem}
\end{eqnarray*}\]



Interpretation of least squares as a projection
Fitted values:
\[
\begin{array}{lcl}
\hat{\mathbf{Y}} &=& \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\\
&=& \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}\\
&=& \mathbf{HY}
\end{array}
\] with \(\mathbf{H}\) the projection matrix also referred to as the hat matrix.

We can also interpret the fit as the projection of the \(n\times 1\) vector \(\mathbf{Y}\) on the column space of the matrix \(\mathbf{X}\).
So each column in \(\mathbf{X}\) is also an \(n\times 1\) vector.
For the toy example n=3 and p=2. The other picture to linear regression is to consider \(X_0\), \(X_1\) and \(Y\) as vectors in the space of the data \(\mathbb{R}^n\), here \(\mathbb{R}^3\) because we have three data points. So the column space of X is a plane in the three dimensional space.

\[
\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{Y}
\]

\(\mathbf{Y}\) is projected in the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\)! spanned by the columns.


How does this projection works?
\[
\begin{array}{lcl}
\hat{\mathbf{Y}} &=& \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}\\
&=& \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1/2}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1/2}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}\\
&=& \mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^T\mathbf{Y}
\end{array}
\]

\(\mathbf{U}\) is a new orthonormal basis in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\)
The space spanned by U and X is the column space of X, e.g. it contains all possible linear combinantions of X. \(\mathbf{U}^t\mathbf{Y}\) is the projection of Y on this new orthonormal basis

5.3.4 Error
Note, that it is also clear from the equation in the derivation of the least squares solution that the residual is orthogonal on the column space:
\[
-2 \mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) = 0
\]

title: Recap general linear model
text:
5.4 Variance Estimator?
\[
\begin{array}{ccl}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}
&=&\text{var}\left[(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{Y}\right]\\\\
&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\text{var}\left[\mathbf{Y}\right]\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\\\\
&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{I}\sigma^2)\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\\\\
&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{I}\quad\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\sigma^2\\\\
%\hat{\boldmath{\Sigma}}_{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\var\left[\mathbf{Y}\right](\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}\\
&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\sigma^2\\\\
&=&(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\sigma^2
\end{array}
\]

title: Recap general linear model
text:
5.5 Contrasts
Hypotheses often involve linear combinations of the model parameters!
e.g.

\(H_0: \log_2{FC}_{g3n1-g1n1}= \beta_{g3} + \hat\beta_{g3n1}=0\) \(\rightarrow\) “grade3+grade3:node1 = 0”
Let \[
\boldsymbol{\beta} = \left[
\begin{array}{c}
\beta_{0}\\
\beta_{g3}\\
\beta_{n1}\\
\beta_{g3:n1}
\end{array}
\right]\]
we can write that contrast using a contrast matrix: \[
\mathbf{L}=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\1\\0\\1\end{array}\right] \rightarrow \mathbf{L}^T\boldsymbol{\beta} \]
Then the variance becomes: \[
\text{var}_{\mathbf{L}^T\boldsymbol{\hat\beta}}= \mathbf{L}^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\hat\beta}}\mathbf{L}
\]

title: Introduction to proteomics data analysis - MaxQuant Data Dependent Acquisition spike-in study
text:
Label-Free Quantitative mass spectrometry based workflows for differential expression (DE) analysis of proteins is often challenging due to peptide-specific effects and context-sensitive missingness of peptide intensities.

msqrob2 provides peptide-based workflows that can assess for DE directly from peptide intensities and outperform summarisation methods which first aggregate MS1 peptide intensities to protein intensities before DE analysis. However, they are computationally expensive, often hard to understand for the non-specialised end-user, and they do not provide protein summaries, which are important for visualisation or downstream processing.
msqrob2 therefore also proposes a novel summarisation strategy, which estimates MSqRob’s model parameters in a two-stage procedure circumventing the drawbacks of peptide-based workflows.
the summarisation based workflow in msqrob2 maintains MSqRob’s superior performance, while providing useful protein expression summaries for plotting and downstream analysis. Summarising peptide to protein intensities considerably reduces the computational complexity, the memory footprint and the model complexity. Moreover, it renders the analysis framework to become modular, providing users the flexibility to develop workflows tailored towards specific applications.

In this vignette we will demonstrate how to perform msqrob’s summarisation based workflow starting from a MaxQuant search on a subset of the cptac spike-in study.
Examples on our peptide-based workflows and on the analysis of more complex designs can be found on our companion website msqrob2 book.
Technical details on our methods can be found in (Goeminne et al. 2016), (Goeminne et al. 2020), (Sticker et al. 2020) and (Vandenbulcke et al. 2025).

Upon installation:

Open RStudio, you will see the following window
